hints: Focus on the shape of the graph, the sharp peaks followed by a sudden drop are the key landmarks for noble gases and alkali metals.
Notice that P is a high peak and Q is the very low point straight after it, so P ends one period and Q starts the next one.
Count the eight elements from Q to X as one full period from Group 1 to Group 0, then see which position V occupies in that sequence.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Noble Gases**

The highest points on a first ionisation energy plot are always the noble gases. They have a stable full shell, so a lot of energy is needed to remove an electron.

So $P$ and $X$ are noble gases (Group 0).

**Spot the Start of a New Period**

Right after a noble gas, the next electron goes into a new shell further from the nucleus. Ionisation energy drops sharply.

So $Q$, the very low point after $P$, is an alkali metal (Group 1) starting a new period.

**Map the Period Q to X**

From $Q$ to $X$ we can count eight consecutive elements. This is the Period 2 sequence Li to Ne:
$$Q(Li) \to R(Be) \to S(B) \to T(C) \to U(N) \to V(O) \to W(F) \to X(Ne)$$

**Place Element V**

Count to the 6th element in that period. $V$ is oxygen with configuration $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$.

An element with 6 outer electrons is in Group 16, which confirms the correct statement.

options.A: Incorrect. P is a peak, not a trough. Peaks are noble gases in Group 0 with very high first ionisation energy, while alkali metals like Q are the low points after the drop.
options.B: Incorrect. R is the second element after Q, so it is beryllium in Group 2 with configuration $1s^2 2s^2$. Group 13 is the third element S (boron), where the dip occurs due to the start of the p subshell.
options.C: Incorrect. U is the fifth element in the Q to X period. It shows a small local peak because of the stable half-filled $2p^3$ arrangement of nitrogen, which is in Group 15, not Group 14.
options.D: Correct. V is the sixth element in the Q to X period, straight after the nitrogen peak U. The dip at V is due to spin-pair repulsion in oxygen, $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$, which places it in Group 16.
